en: Dr. Fe del Mundo invented a bamboo incubator to keep premature babies warm and safe in rural areas without electricity.
National hero Jose Rizal cultivated and studied medicinal plants like guava and eucalyptus in Dapitan to treat local illnesses.
The Ifugao built stone-walled rice terraces that prevent soil erosion and protect mountain communities from dangerous landslides during heavy rains.
The 1987 Philippine Constitution mandates the state to protect the ecology, ensuring citizens have the right to breathe clean air and drink safe water.
During loud Philippine festivals like Sinulog, wearing earplugs protects your eardrums from permanent noise-induced hearing loss caused by booming drums.
The Department of Health recognizes lagundi, a native Philippine shrub, as a scientifically proven herbal medicine for coughs and asthma.
Local government units enforce solid waste laws requiring households to segregate trash to prevent dengue-carrying mosquitoes from breeding in stagnant water.
Understanding the physics of typhoon storm surges helps communities apply the value of bayanihan to safely evacuate coastal residents before severe flooding.
In 1901, the Bureau of Health applied emerging microbiology and sanitation science to combat deadly infectious diseases like cholera in the Philippines.
The Manobo people traditionally use the antimicrobial bark of the narra tree to safely clean wounds and prevent bacterial infections.
The Executive branch monitors typhoons using PAGASA to apply meteorological science and issue timely public storm warning signals for public safety.
National Artist Guillermo Tolentino used structurally sound bronze and marble to ensure his monuments safely withstand earthquakes and harsh weather.
